messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Since the exposure, Kwame, a 62-year-old bomb disposal technician, has described his world as permanently edged with danger. The incident happened at work during what had first seemed like a controlled response to a suspicious device in an industrial setting. When the container was opened, it released a toxic chemical plume before the team could fully contain it. He remembers the sharp, sterile-burning smell in the air, the confusion of shouted instructions, and the abrupt sense that his own body had become unsafe terrain. In the aftermath he was taken through medical evaluation, surrounded by antiseptic odors and emergency activity that have remained fused in his mind with the moment he realized he might not be able to protect himself. What stays vivid for him is not only the exposure itself, but the feeling that danger was invisible, already in the air, and could reach him before he had time to react.

In the weeks afterward, the workplace itself became charged for him. Entering the facility, hearing sudden loud noises, or catching even a faint hospital or antiseptic smell could pull him into the same tense, immediate alarm. He found that these moments did not just upset him; they changed what he did. He began avoiding medical settings whenever possible, putting off examinations and steering away from hospitals and ambulances because the sights and smells felt too close to the exposure. He also started arranging his days so that he was rarely by himself in a room or building, and when he could not avoid those situations he felt markedly less steady. Most of all, he worked excessively. Staying busy on the job made sense to him because it kept him from sitting alone with the memories and bodily tension that seemed to gather the minute the environment reminded him of what had happened.

Those same reminders also kept his body and attention in a state of readiness. At work, a loud metallic bang or an unexpected sound in the bay would make him jerk and immediately search the area, and he noticed that once he was keyed up he could not stop scanning for signs of danger. In any building, including restaurants or his church, he was uncomfortable until he had identified the exits and decided how he would get out if something went wrong. The antiseptic smell of clinics was especially potent; even passing a medical office was enough to make him more vigilant, more aware of who was near him, and more likely to react sharply if someone touched him without warning. His wife has learned not to come up behind him because he startles so intensely that he feels embarrassed and angry afterward.

Over time, this constant watchfulness seemed to make the reminders spread. Because Kwame was already scanning his surroundings and mapping escape routes before he felt at ease, ordinary parts of the workplace stood out to him as possible signs of threat. A routine noise he might once have ignored now caught his full attention and felt loaded. When he was tense, even a cleaning product with a sterile scent could register as if it belonged to an emergency room, and he would feel himself transported back into the atmosphere of the exposure. The more alert he stayed, the easier it became for the workplace, loud sounds, and medical smells to set him off again.

His ways of coping have tightened that pattern rather than easing it. By avoiding hospitals and examinations, he gets short-term relief, but he remains convinced those places are unbearable and dangerous to enter. By refusing to be alone, he never has the chance to discover that solitude itself is not the threat he feels it to be; instead he stays on edge whenever separation seems possible. Overworking has narrowed his life further. He takes extra shifts and lingers at work rather than going home early, telling himself it is better to stay occupied than to be left with his thoughts. Yet the fatigue leaves him even more jumpy, more likely to react to a touch on the shoulder, and more dependent on scanning and exit planning to feel barely in control. His wife has begun to complain that even when he is physically home, he is not really with her, just watching the room.

By the time he sought help, Kwame was exhausted by how small and effortful his life had become. He could still function in his highly specialized job, but only by staying in motion and never letting his guard down. What finally brought him in was the recognition that he was organizing every setting around escape, every day around avoiding reminders, and still feeling as if the danger could break through at any moment. He says he wants to stop living “like the leak is still happening.” What frightens him most is the possibility that if he stops monitoring and pushing himself, he will be caught off guard again. What he hopes, cautiously, is that he might be able to be in a room by himself, hear an abrupt noise, or walk past a hospital without feeling that his body has already been overtaken.
